articles.title: What's next for SpaceX's Starship after epic Flight 15 chopsticks catch?
articles.author: Mike Wall

paras.en: Starship may have just made history, but it still has some work to do to get fully up and running.

The megarocket launched on its 15th test flight on Friday (Nov. 13), aiming to pull off a dramatic and unprecedented twofer. SpaceX wanted to bring both Starship elements — its Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage — back to the launch pad at its Starbase site in Texas to be caught by the tower's "chopstick" arms.

It didn't happen with Super Heavy; the booster diverted to a Gulf of Mexico splashdown on Friday evening after experiencing a low-fuel alarm. But Ship came home successfully, nestling into the tower's arms in a soft and unprecedented embrace on Saturday afternoon (Nov. 14), 22.5 hours after lifting off.

SpaceX has caught Super Heavy on three test flights to date. But it had never caught a Ship before; indeed, it had never even tried before Saturday. It's tougher and riskier to catch Ship; the upper stage flies much higher and faster than Super Heavy, so its return trip is much more more involved.
Saturday was therefore a very big day for the company.

"That was the holy grail of spaceflight, plummeting through fire to be snatched out of the air by steel," SpaceX spokesperson Dan Huot said during the company's landing webcast on Saturday. "We caught a Starship, and now everything changes."

The Flight 15 mission plan gave us a sneak peek at the future: The double catch will be standard on operational Starship missions, as this recovery strategy will enable rapid inspection, refurbishment and reflight of the megarocket, according to SpaceX.

And the company is indeed planning on rapid reflight. Elon Musk has said that SpaceX is targeting 10,000 Starship launches per year by 2030, which works out to more than one liftoff every hour on average.

Why such a mind-boggling cadence? Because SpaceX plans to build megaconstellations far larger than anything circling Earth today. For example, it wants its next-gen Starlink V3 broadband network to consist of 100,000 satellites. And its planned Starmind AI data-center constellation will be 10 times bigger than that, featuring one million spacecraft, if all goes to plan.
For perspective: SpaceX's current-gen Starlink network in low Earth orbit (LEO), by far the largest constellation ever assembled, is about 11,000 strong at the moment.

Rocket recovery is only part of the reuse equation, of course; there's also refurbishment and reflight. And that gets us back to the "work left to do" discussion, for SpaceX has yet to demonstrate rapid reflight with either Super Heavy or Ship.

The company has reflown Super Heavy vehicles on two separate occasions. Booster 14 initially launched on Flight 7 in January 2025, then lifted off again on Flight 9 in May of that year. Booster 15 flew on Flight 8 and Flight 11, which lifted off in March 2025 and October 2025, respectively.
Several months separated each of these Super Heavy reflights. And SpaceX has yet to reuse a Ship, as it had not caught one during a mission until Saturday.
That could change soon: Before Flight 15 lifted off, Musk said that the company wants to reuse both of its Starship stages. That option may still be on the table for Flight 15's Ship.

And we should expect full reuse to be a priority on Starship test flights over the longer haul, with SpaceX working toward shorter and shorter turnaround times — perhaps until an hourly cadence is in sight, if that goal is indeed achievable.

Over the next few years, most Starship launches will likely be devoted to building out the Starlink V3 and Starmind megaconstellations. But the rocket will also carry people to deep space, if all goes to plan, which will require the checking of another set of boxes.

NASA selected Ship to be the first crewed lunar lander for its Artemis program, which aims to establish a base near the lunar south pole by 2032 or so. Current plans call for Ship to land astronauts in that locale for the first time on the Artemis IV mission, which is targeted to fly in 2028.

SpaceX needs to install a crew cabin and life-support system in Ship to make that happen. The company is working on that now and has made considerable progress, according to NASA. Last month, an agency presentation reported that SpaceX is on target to finish building "Cabin 1," a full-scale ground prototype of Ship's crew cabin, by the end of the year.

There's another hurdle to clear, however. On all deep-space missions, Ship will need to fill up its fuel tanks after launch, at a "depot" that SpaceX will set up in Earth orbit. (Launching Ship with full tanks is not an option, as it would be incredibly heavy in that case.)

The depot will be filled by "tanker" variants of Ship. It's unclear how many tanker visits will be required for each Ship deep-space mission; outside experts have floated numbers as high as 22, while Musk has cited six to eight as a probable range.

Whatever the actual number, Ship will need to demonstrate proficiency with off-Earth refueling, something it has yet to do. And there's more to it than just a simple rendezvous: Ship's engines run on liquid oxygen and liquid methane, so the propellants must be kept extremely cold throughout the process.

We're likely to see the first refueling test relatively soon, as time is of the essence for SpaceX. If the company can't get Ship ready for the Artemis IV moon landing in 2028, NASA may go with another private lander — Blue Origin's Blue Moon, which the agency also contracted for Artemis missions.
All of this is to say that, while Flight 15 was a big success for Starship and SpaceX, there's a lot of work left to do — and a lot for space fans to watch for over the coming weeks and months.

Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. To find out what his latest project is, you can follow Michael on Twitter.

articles.title: How escaping gases ripped apart a comet and caused it to become thousands of times brighter
articles.author: Keith Cooper

paras.en: A comet dazzled this summer as the sun’s heat caused ice beneath its surface to turn to gas and rip out through its surface, spewing hundreds of billions of pounds' worth of dust into space and causing the comet to brighten by thousands of times.

Comet 220P/McNaught was discovered by the prolific Australian comet discoverer Robert McNaught in 2004. It is a periodic comet, the 220th discovered, meaning that it comes back again and again on a regular basis – in 220P’s case, once every five-and-a-half years when it gets about as close to the sun as Mars. Other than that, 220P is fairly nondescript, usually languishing at a feeble brightness fainter than magnitude +15, out of reach of most amateur telescopes. There has been little else to say about the comet, until this year.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: On June 14, as it headed towards perihelion – the closest point in its orbit to the sun, at a distance from our star of 1.5 times the distance between the Earth and the sun (known as an astronomical unit), 220P suddenly and without warning burst into life.

On 31 May, the comet was languishing at magnitude +17.39 (the higher the magnitude, the fainter an object is), but within less than 14 hours it had dramatically brightened to magnitude +11.05, bringing it into range for observation with small amateur telescopes.

By June 2, 220P was up to magnitude +8.23 and was technically visible for a short while in 10x50 binoculars from a dark site, prompting amateur astronomers and astrophotographers to chase down this rare event.
By perihelion, the comet had faded back to magnitude +12, but more was to come. A second outburst began at the end of July, brightening from magnitude +14 on 28 July to magnitude 6.1 by 6 August.

Comets are often referred to as dirty snowballs, and beneath their dusty crust are ices made from various volatiles, including water, carbon dioxide and nitrogen. Solar heating, even at the distance of Mars, can cause these ices to rapidly sublimate into gases, and the pressure of the escaping gas rips the surface apart, spewing huge amounts of dust in to space.

Models based on observations of 220P’s outburst indicate that it spewed out between tens of billions and hundreds of billions of pounds’ worth of cometary dust that filled the comet’s coma, the diffuse 'atmosphere' that clings to the comet’s solid nucleus. The dust particles, which are just millionths of a meter across, expanded outwards from the comet at about 1,280 feet (390 meters) per second, scattering sunlight and causing the coma to substantially brighten.

"We have concluded that the comet detached localized parts of its crust, creating a dust-rich envelope that increased [the comet’s brightness by] 250 times in half a day," Josep M. Trigo-Rodríguez, of the Institut de Ciències de l’Espai and the Institute of Space Studies of Catalonia in Spain, said in a statement.
While this is the first time that 220P has been seen to outburst, over the years we have witnessed other comets spectacularly brighten out of nowhere.

A recent and well-known example is comet 17P/Holmes, which brightened a million-fold in the fall of 2007 as it rose from magnitude +17 to magnitude +2.8, becoming a welcome naked-eye sight in the constellation of Perseus for many people as they made the evening commute home.
The short 5.5-year orbit of 220P marks it out as a Jupiter-family comet.

"Jupiter-family comets are extremely interesting objects to study because they originate primarily from the Kuiper Belt and the Scattered Disk region, later migrating inward until Jupiter captures them into short-period orbits," said Trigo-Rodríguez.

Studying outbursts such as the two experienced by 220P provides vital clues as to the bulk characteristics of Jupiter-family comets, giving us insight into objects that originated from beyond the orbit of Neptune.
Of particular interest to Trigo-Rodríguez is what we should do were one of these objects ever to be found on a collision course with Earth.

"Particularly we are interested in the tensile strength and nature of comets in the framework of our studies on impact hazards," said Trigo-Rodríguez. "Some comets seem determined to demonstrate that they are fragile enough and perhaps give us the chance to invoke disruptive approaches that might be substantially different from the ones already tested or proposed for asteroids."

For now, 220P is heading back out to its furthest point from the sun, which is just inside the orbit of Jupiter at a distance of 4.68 astronomical units or 435 million miles (700 million kilometers). Having passed as close to Earth as it is going to get this time around on 12 October at a distance of 1.04 astronomical units or 97 million miles (156 million kilometres), the comet is currently magnitude +13 and fading. All eyes will be on 220P during its next time around the sun in late 2031.
The findings were published on Nov.3 in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society.

Keith Cooper is a freelance science journalist and editor in the United Kingdom, and has a degree in physics and astrophysics from the University of Manchester. He's the author of "The Contact Paradox: Challenging Our Assumptions in the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence" (Bloomsbury Sigma, 2020) and has written articles on astronomy, space, physics and astrobiology for a multitude of magazines and websites.

articles.title: Horizon Microtechnologies Targets Constellation-Scale Production As Esa Phi-Lab Selection Strengthens Industrialisation Push
articles.author: Horizon Microtechnologies

paras.en: (Karlsruhe, Germany, September 29th 2026) Horizon Microtechnologies is accelerating industrialisation of its metallised polymer micro-additive manufacturing platform through IP-MASS, a two-year scale-up project supported by €500,000 and reinforced by selection for ESA Phi-Lab Austria.

The programme is expanding Horizon’s printing, coating and process-verification capabilities for shielding housings and other passive RF hardware, targeting up to 50,000 precision-coated satellite components and a repeatable manufacturing framework suited to constellation-class demand rather than one-off prototype production.

Horizon combines precision polymer 3D printing with conformal metallisation and protective coatings. Polymer provides the precision bulk geometry, while metal is applied only to the thickness required. Replacing even lightweight metals such as aluminium with metallised polymer can reduce weight by 40%, while 3D printing can deliver further size, weight and design advantages alongside attractive economics compared with conventionally machined metal parts.

ESA Phi-Lab Austria’s “Industrialization by Design” focus supports upstream space technologies with commercial potential, reflecting the move towards scalable, reliable and cost-effective industrial products.

Importantly, IP-MASS is not limited to shielding housings. Horizon is also seeking spacecraft and space-related terrestrial applications where polymer 3D printing and metallisation could address product requirements, manufacturing constraints or future volume demand.

“Horizon has proved that metallised polymer micro-AM can deliver far more than lightweight prototypes,” said Andreas Frölich, CEO of Horizon Microtechnologies. “The next challenge is industrial: achieving the prices, lead times, repeatability and throughput needed when a component is required not once or ten times, but thousands or tens of thousands of times.”

Frölich adds, “Shielding housings give us a strong first industrialisation case, but they are not the limit. We also want to address components where lightweight printed geometry and functional metallic surfaces could create a meaningful technical or manufacturing advantage.”

The move builds on Horizon’s space-readiness work, which subjected representative metallised polymer demonstrators to established LEO tests including outgassing, temperature shock, radiation, mechanical shock, material fatigue and atomic-oxygen exposure.

For high-volume satellite architectures such as phased-array payloads, components may be used hundreds of times per spacecraft and across hundreds of satellites, turning component-level mass and cost savings into significant programme-level gains.

IP-MASS also provides scope to cooperate on applications with anticipated demand of 100 units per year or more. Partners do not need a fully developed component: early-stage concepts are welcome while design-for-manufacturability decisions can still be made.

“We do not want to assume that we already know every application where this technology can create value,” Frölich says. “The organisations designing next-generation spacecraft know where their product and manufacturing constraints are. We want them to bring those challenges to us so we can explore whether the technology is relevant and, where it is, potentially shape the manufacturing route together.”

Horizon is moving beyond validation towards an industrial manufacturing platform for next-generation satellite hardware, while inviting the space community to help identify which applications it should industrialise next.

Horizon is a member of the Green Space Center, an initiative supported by the State of Baden-Württemberg and based at the Chamber of Commerce and Industry Reutlingen (IHK Reutlingen) that promotes innovation in water management, New Space, and intelligent systems.

“We help SMEs in Baden-Württemberg internationalize space-related business models and products and support their entry into international markets,” said Marcin Bielecki, Head of Technology at the Green Space Center.

The initiative aims to position Baden-Württemberg as a sustainability-driven hub for space technology by fostering cross-sector collaboration and applying space technologies to create ecological impact.

Baden-Württemberg hosts a dynamic and rapidly growing New Space ecosystem, including leading European companies such as ATMOS Space Cargo, HyImpulse, ConstellR and CELERES while supporting emerging innovators such as InSpacePropulsion Technologies (ISPTech) and Yugen Space.

articles.title: Moog Marks 25 Years Since ESPA Design Milestone: Innovating Space Rideshare
articles.author: Moog Inc.

paras.en: East Aurora, N.Y. — Moog Inc. (NYSE: MOG.A and MOG.B) marks 25 years since the Evolved Secondary Payload Adapter (ESPA) ring completed its Critical Design Review in 2001. The pioneering technology helped advance space rideshare by enabling multiple payloads to share a launch and broadening access to orbit for commercial, government, and defense missions.

Development of ESPA began in 1999 through a collaborative government-industry initiative, culminating in the successful completion of its Critical Design Review on January 18, 2001. The ESPA ring enabled launch vehicles to carry multiple secondary payloads by efficiently using previously unused volume beneath primary satellites. This approach lowered costs and increased mission flexibility, supporting commercial satellite constellations, technology demonstrations, and critical defense operations.

paras.en: “ESPA helped redefine access to space by enabling additional payloads to share a launch with primary missions. Its impact continues across commercial, government, and military space—and its story reflects the value of enduring collaboration between Air Force Research Lab (AFRL) and industry partners such as Moog,” said Dr. Darren Raspa, chief historian, AFRL Space and Directed Energy Systems.

Over the past 25 years, the ESPA family has evolved into a versatile, modular platform supporting varied payload sizes and interface configurations. ESPA-derived designs have also served as the structural foundation for spacecraft buses. Today, the platform continues to support mission planning for NASA, the U.S. government, and commercial space ventures worldwide.

Moog continues to offer a family of ESPA configurations, including Standard ESPA, ESPA Heavy, and ESPA Grande, designed to accommodate evolving payload and mission requirements. The platform’s modular architecture and adaptable interfaces support rideshare missions, payload integration, and spacecraft applications across the growing space market.

“The ESPA ring began as a technical solution to a practical challenge: maximizing every launch opportunity,” said Timothy Pargett, general manager, Moog Payload Adapters and Isolation business. “Today, it stands as a cornerstone of how missions, large and small, gain cost-effective, reliable access to orbit through rideshare. Its enduring legacy reflects visionary innovation and trusted partnerships across the aerospace community.”

In conjunction with the anniversary, a Moog flight-qualified ESPA ring will be on display at the National Museum of Nuclear Science & History in Albuquerque, N.M., from November 7, 2026, through January 10, 2027.
Museum visitors will have the opportunity to see firsthand the hardware that helped advance rideshare and enable diverse space missions.

As ESPA enters its next chapter, Moog continues to advance spacecraft payload integration and develop adaptable solutions that expand flexible, cost-effective access to orbit for future space exploration and defense missions.

Moog is a worldwide designer, manufacturer, and systems integrator of high-performance precision motion and fluid controls and control systems. Moog’s high-performance systems control military and commercial aircraft, satellites, and space vehicles, launch vehicles, defense systems, missiles, automated industrial machinery, marine, and medical equipment. Additional information about the Company can be found at www.moog.com or www.moog.com/space.

articles.title: Senate committee takes up nominees for NASA chief financial officer and inspector general
articles.author: Jeff Foust

paras.en: WASHINGTON — A Senate committee is set to advance nominations for NASA’s chief financial officer and inspector general.

The Senate Commerce Committee held a hearing Nov. 10 to consider nominations for several posts, including that of Joshua Shoemaker to be NASA’s chief financial officer and Robert Steinau to be inspector general. Those are two of the four positions at the agency that require Senate confirmation; the others are administrator and deputy administrator.

Neither nominee received many questions during the hearing, which lasted a little more than an hour. Senators largely focused their attention on the nomination of Danielle Thumann to be a member of the Federal Communications Commission.

Shoemaker is an accountant who has worked for more than 20 years in the private sector and in the Mississippi state government. Since August, he has been a senior adviser in NASA’s Mission Support Directorate, and before that was controller for the Republican National Committee.

Steinau has worked since 2009 at NASA’s Office of Inspector General, and since December 2024 has served as the office’s senior official in the absence of a Senate-confirmed inspector general. He previously worked for the Department of Energy’s Office of Inspector General and for the U.S. Secret Service.

Shoemaker, in his opening statement at the nomination hearing, said he would focus on financial accountability, improved visibility into financial performance of NASA programs, transparency with Congress on that performance and modernization of NASA financial systems.

“I believe the CFO has an important responsibility to give the administrator, NASA leadership and Congress an honest and timely picture of the agency’s financial position,” he said. He added that means how programs are performing against their planned budgets and schedules as well as ensuring effective management of resources.

He deferred questions on specific programs as well as on the proposed U.S. Space Academy that a presidential commission, led by NASA, is studying. Shoemaker said that decisions on locating the academy will ultimately be made by the president.

Steinau said that, as inspector general, he would focus on three critical challenges for NASA: returning humans to the moon, transitioning from the International Space Station to commercial stations and cybersecurity.
“NASA is moving with urgency, and it is imperative that accountability keep pace with ambition,” he said.
The Senate Commerce Committee announced Nov. 11 that it will meet Nov. 18 to vote on the nominees at the Nov. 10 hearing, sending them, if approved, to the full Senate for a confirmation vote.

NASA has been without a Senate-confirmed chief financial officer since the start of the Trump administration in January 2025. The White House nominated Greg Autry for that position in the spring of 2025, but the nomination was returned by the Senate without acting on it at the end of the year. NASA has lacked a Senate-confirmed inspector general since the departure of Paul Martin in late 2023.

articles.title: The Last Ice on Puncak Jaya

paras.en: On the island of New Guinea, Indonesia’s Sudirman Range is one of the few places near the equator that have long held ice year-round. But near the summit of Puncak Jaya, the ice has dwindled to patches too small to flow like glaciers.

Positioned in the tropics beside the largest expanse of warm ocean water on Earth, the range’s glaciers lie near the warmest conditions in which ice can survive year-round. Scientists have described these glaciers as high-altitude “canaries in the coal mine,” alongside other tropical ice such as the remnants of Humboldt Glacier in Venezuela, Quelccaya Ice Cap in Peru, and the ice fields of Kilimanjaro in Tanzania.

The change on Puncak Jaya is visible in this image pair, acquired in 1988 by the TM (Thematic Mapper) on Landsat 5 (left) and in 2026 by the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 (right). The false-color images help distinguish areas of ice (light blue) from exposed bedrock (brown). Clouds appear white and vegetation green.

In 1988, the glaciers covered about 4.31 square kilometers (1.66 square miles), according to Donaldi Permana, a climate scientist at the Indonesian Agency for Meteorology, Climatology, and Geophysics (BMKG). By September 2025, satellite and aerial data showed that only about 0.09 square kilometers (0.03 square miles) remained—an area equivalent to about a dozen soccer fields. That’s roughly 2 percent of the 1988 extent. An aerial survey planned for December should yield an estimate of how much ice remains in 2026, Permana said.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The glaciers have thinned, too. Measurements at the primary monitoring site on the East Northwall Firn showed a drop from 32 meters (105 feet) thick in 2010 to 4 meters (13 feet) in 2023, Permana said. By November 2024, the ice at this site was gone.

As the glaciers thin, they also break apart, and each new fragment adds exposed edges where ice can melt, compounding the losses. In the 2026 Landsat image, freshly uncovered bedrock appears between the remnants. Snow still falls in the area, but it doesn’t last long enough on the bare rock to build up into new ice.

“It’s a house of cards problem,” said Chris Shuman, a retired University of Maryland glaciologist who has tracked Puncak Jaya’s glaciers in satellite imagery. “Once this process gets going, there’s really no turning back.”

To qualify as a glacier, a body of ice generally has to be thick enough to flow downhill under its own weight, and it needs an area where snow builds up faster than it melts. Puncak Jaya’s remaining ice has thinned so much and broken into such small, stagnant patches that it no longer flows.
“While small ice remnants persist in high-altitude crevices around Puncak Jaya, their functional life as active glaciers is effectively over,” Permana said.

As for the remaining patches of ice, time will tell how long they last. Recent satellite studies suggest complete disappearance of the main glacial ice areas could occur around 2030. Permana noted that BMKG estimates suggest they could be gone much sooner, hastened by the current El Niño.

Past El Niño years have hit these glaciers especially hard. As the air warms, the freezing level rises above the summit, so precipitation falls as rain instead of snow. That means less fresh white snow that normally reflects sunlight and shields the ice, leaving darker surfaces that absorb more heat and melt faster. During the 2015-2016 El Niño, the ice thinned about five times faster than usual, losing roughly 5.3 meters (17 feet) of thickness in a single year. The 2023-2024 El Niño brought another bout of rapid thinning, about 2 to 4 meters (7 to 13 feet) per year.

articles.title: APOD: 2026 November 16 – NGC 7129: Star Formation with Jets from Webb

paras.en: Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer.
NGC 7129: Star Formation with Jets from Webb

Explanation: How do stars form? To help answer this question, NASA used the James Webb Space Telescope to take the featured detailed image of the star-forming region NGC 7129 in infrared light. Star formation progresses when gravity pulls together massive amounts of gas, but soon things can get complicated when previously formed stars emit powerful jets and winds -- and some then explode. Opaque dust can form in the cool atmospheres of stars and, when dispersed, can obstruct visible-light images. Many stars can be seen to be forming in the featured image, with the young stars on the left, in the gold-colored gas, typically being more mature than the young stars on the right -- in the red region. Jets and winds likely cause the filamentary nature of the red-colored gas. Studying stars at different stages of development bolsters understanding about what physical processes are most important and when.

articles.title: COP31: New initiative targets AI and reliable climate change information

paras.en: COP31: New initiative targets AI and reliable climate change information

New guidance has been issued to ensure that people everywhere can obtain credible climate change information from artificial intelligence (AI) and understand how the technology impacts the environment.

The Priorities for Action on AI and Climate Information Integrity were launched at the COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Türkiye, on Friday by the Global Initiative for Information Integrity on Climate Change, which is co-chaired by the United Nations, its scientific agency UNESCO and Brazil.

“The question isn't simply whether AI is good or bad for the climate. It’s whether people can rely on what they’re told by AI and about it,” said Charlotte Scaddan, Information Integrity Senior Advisor with the UN Department of Global Communications.

Although more people are turning to AI for climate information, the co-chairs note that the Independent International Scientific Panel on AI – established last year by the UN General Assembly – has warned that “producing fluent text is easier than producing factual text” for the revolutionary tech.

Moreover, risks can increase during climate disasters, when AI-generated images and videos can spread faster than official warnings. Meanwhile, the general public is asked to accept claims about AI’s own climate impact while lacking the necessary data to evaluate its effect on the environment.
The global priorities seek to uphold accountability and transparency.
They call for AI companies to assess how their systems affect climate information integrity, to publish their findings and disclose their energy use and carbon, water and land footprints.
At the same time, States are urged to integrate information integrity into national AI strategies and climate plans.

The action points are grounded in human rights and build on the Belém Declaration on Information Integrity on Climate Change, launched during COP30 last year in Brazil, and the UN Global Principles for Information Integrity.

The partners in the initiative called for greater investment in the information people use to understand and act on climate change. So far, Germany has committed more than $2.2 million to support research, develop communication strategies and undertake public awareness campaigns.

Friday also marked the launch of the Charter for Climate Information Integrity in Advertising which seeks to address problems such as “monetization of disinformation and denial”, said Jake Dubbins, co-founder of the Conscious Advertising Network.
The charter calls for transparency across the advertising supply chain to ensure that advertisers have visibility of ad placements while respecting user privacy.
COP31 is focused around 10 priority themes, including clean energy transition and electrification, zero waste and climate-resilient cities. The conference concludes on 20 November.

articles.title: ‘Lives are at stake’: Humanitarians call for swift entry of winter supplies in Gaza

paras.en: ‘Lives are at stake’: Humanitarians call for swift entry of winter supplies in Gaza
“The devastating impact of the latest rainstorm in Gaza was preventable,” the Humanitarian Country Team (HCT) in the Occupied Palestinian Territory said in a statement.
“Children and adults were killed, critical services suspended, and thousands of family shelters flooded, swept away, or torn apart – not by the storm alone, but by policy decisions.”

The HCT brings together heads of UN agencies and international and local non-governmental organizations who recalled that several months ago they had presented a plan to help Palestinians prepare for the current winter season.
It outlined what they would deliver, such as shelter, improved health and protection services, drainage and sandbag reinforcement, and identified various supplies that need to enter Gaza.
These include tents, warm clothes and blankets as well as equipment for pumping water, removing debris and clearing explosive ordnance.
The plan also spelled out the need for sufficient funding, expedited entry of critical supplies and access to higher ground.
Their statement underlined Israel’s obligation as the Occupying Power to ensure the basic needs of Gaza’s population, including supplies essential for survival.
“Yet Israeli policies continue to obstruct the entry of critical items as well as access to most of Gaza’s land, including areas away from the shoreline that are less prone to flooding,” they said.
“Incoming supplies face multiple approval requirements, limited crossing capacity and unpredictable or narrow delivery windows that delay their entry.”

They noted that “although funding has fallen far short of what is needed”, more than 150,000 tents are currently outside Gaza waiting to be dispatched. Meanwhile, needs inside the enclave are growing as every rainstorm destroys more tents, requiring more replacements.
“Winter will last for months. Access to longer-lasting shelter must not be made conditional on political progress when people’s needs are so urgent,” they said.
“Winter supplies must reach families immediately to prevent further loss of life and protect their dignity. People cannot wait.”
They called on the Israeli authorities to expedite the entry of life-saving supplies in Gaza, lift restrictions and enable the repair of water and wastewater networks
“Let all humanitarian partners operate – UN agencies, international organizations, and Palestinian NGOs alike. Allow meaningful commercial activity,” they said.

The partners also urged Member States “to use their influence to ensure these steps are taken swiftly and to provide the necessary humanitarian funding without delay”, stressing that “lives are at stake.”

articles.title: ‘Here, you can eat until you’re full’: Oleshky evacuees savour first proper meals in years

paras.en: ‘Here, you can eat until you’re full’: Oleshky evacuees savour first proper meals in years

In a quiet hospital corridor in Kyiv, staff and volunteers push carts carrying steaming pots of chicken soup, bread and buckwheat porridge to patients recently evacuated from Russian-occupied Oleshky, in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region.
For most people, a bowl of soup is unremarkable. But for evacuees like Olha, who spent the last four-and-a-half years trapped in a war zone, the World Food Programme (WFP) meals are a feast.
“Our neighbours had eaten all the pigeons in the area, every last one,” the 50-year-old recalls. “I simply couldn’t understand how there could be hunger in the 21st century.”

Olha is one of hundreds of people evacuated from Oleshky in late October under a brief ceasefire who are now receiving medical check-ups and treatment in Kyiv hospitals. WFP and its Ukrainian partner, Iskra Dobra, were the first humanitarian responders to provide hot meals the moment they arrived.
“This is the first proper meal they have had in years,” said Richard Ragan, WFP Country Director in Ukraine.

When the war erupted in 2022, Oleshky was occupied – sitting on the frontline – and eventually cut off from humanitarian assistance. Olha and her husband, Serhii, were searched, interrogated and threatened. “By noon at the latest, everyone was indoors,” Serhii says.
Food grew scarce and prices soared, and a kilo of flour could cost as much as $12, evacuees say. In May, food deliveries ended altogether.

With no heating in their shell-damaged home, the family slept in three layers of clothes. Olha planted cucumbers, tomatoes and zucchini, rushing outside during brief lulls between attacks to tend them.
“It was terribly frightening. But what could we do? We had to eat,” she says.
Further down the corridor, 78-year-old Valentyna describes how she and her elderly neighbours made soup from wild plants. “There was no bread, no flour, nothing at all,” she says.

“Until we reached the border, we were afraid anything could still happen,” Olha recalls. Then, suddenly, they were through. Along the road to Kyiv, people stood holding signs and Ukrainian flags to welcome them.
“We saw our people,” she says. “There was something so wonderful about their energy. A sense of peace.”
For Valentyna, the meals have been a revelation. “Here, you can eat until you’re full! I hadn’t seen so much food in years,” she says. “The borscht is absolutely delicious.”

Since Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, WFP has provided the equivalent of 4.1 billion meals to Ukraine’s most vulnerable people. Every month, it reaches 357,000 people in frontline communities with emergency food and cash assistance, and some 200,000 students receive its daily school meals.

For the evacuees, the future remains uncertain, with homes they cannot return to and years of fear that will not simply disappear. But there is also the relief of being safe and, in a hospital room in Kyiv, having a hot meal waiting.

articles.title: Khawaja ready to be frozen out by Cricket Australia after sandpaper storm

paras.en: 'Sandpapergate': Usman Khawaja says being frozen out by Cricket Australia 'a small price to pay' for ball-tampering claims, calls bans 'grotesquely overboard'

Usman Khawaja says bans handed out to David Warner, Steve Smith and Cameron Bancroft were "grotesquely overboard" following sandpaper scandal in 2018; Khawaja claims every member of Australia dressing room knew about the plot eight years ago, an allegation vehemently denied by Pat Cummins
Usman Khawaja says being frozen out by Cricket Australia would be a "small price to pay" after his claims about the 2018 ball-tampering affair in South Africa.

Khawaja alleged in his autobiography 'Sabr' that every member of the Australia dressing room was aware of the plot to alter the condition of the ball with sandpaper and not just the players who copped bans in Steve Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft.

The 39-year-old's account has been backed up by former team-mates Warner and Chadd Sayers but vehemently denied by current Test captain Pat Cummins, who was part of the bowling group in the series against the Proteas eight years ago.

Khawaja retired from international cricket after Australia's 4-1 Ashes thrashing of England earlier this year but continues to play for Brisbane Heat in the Big Bash League.
'I have stood up for three guys I feel were treated unfairly'

Speaking on an episode of the They Used to Be podcast, which was recorded before Cummins' called Khawaja's claims about 'Sandpapergate' "100 per cent wrong and "utter nonsense", the batter said: "I still have a very good relationship with (Cricket Australia chief executive) Todd Greenberg.
"What happens to that relationship in the future, honestly [I don't know]. If Cricket Australia for some reason doesn't want to, it's a small price to pay in my mind for doing what I did.
"I have stood up for three guys I feel were treated unfairly (Warner, Smith and Bancroft).
"But there are other guys that are still playing in the team right now that there might be some sort of cost. I have tried my best to balance that out.
"There is always a cost in everything you do. There has been a cost to my family, too. But I am also not playing the victim here, because I knew what I was getting into.
"I knew what was coming. I just didn't realise it would be so personal."
Khawaja: 'Sandpapergate' bans were 'grotesquely overboard'
On the podcast, Khawaja spoke of an "awkward" conversation with Smith before the release of his book.

He also called the penalties dished out following the sandpaper storm as "grotesquely overboard" and "over the top" with then-skipper Smith and vice-captain Warner hit with year-long suspensions and Bancroft banned for nine months.
Warner was also told he could not captain again before that sanction was lifted years later.
Khawaja added: "I'm not here to say 'he did this', 'that person did that, or 'he knew this or he knew that'.
"It was more a case of 'we win as a team, we lose as a team, we take chances as a team'. I think if there is an opportunity to do that, we can move forward once and for all."

articles.title: 'All the force!' - Mercedes open to prioritising Russell in final races

paras.en: Toto Wolff says Mercedes could prioritise George Russell over Kimi Antonelli in final races of 2026 F1 season from Las Vegas GP

Mercedes hoping for a one-two in the Drivers' Championship to go with dual title triumph; Kimi Antonelli already champion but George Russell currently third; watch the Las Vegas GP weekend on Sky Sports F1, with qualifying at 4am on Saturday and the race at 4am on Sunday
Toto Wolff says Mercedes could throw their weight behind George Russell over the final three races of the season to help him finish second in the Drivers' Championship.

Mercedes have already secured a world championship double this year, with Kimi Antonelli clinching the drivers' title in Mexico before the team wrapped up the constructors' crown a week later in Brazil.

But a difficult run of results for Russell since his last win at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix in September has seen the Briton slip out of the top two in the Drivers' Championship. He is third, 17 points behind Red Bull's Max Verstappen in second and only one point ahead of Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton in fourth.

Speaking after the Sao Paulo Grand Prix, Wolff was asked whether, with both titles now won, Mercedes would prioritise Russell over the final three rounds to help get him back into second place behind Antonelli.
"I haven't thought about the driver championship yet, but we absolutely want him to score the maximum and hopefully finish second," said the Mercedes team principal.
"And we need to think about what we're going to do about it.
"But it could be a possibility that we're giving it all the force."

Pre-season title favourite Russell has endured a disappointing season in which under-performance relative to Antonelli and misfortune have combined to leave him more than 100 points behind his team-mate.
But Wolff is expecting the 28-year-old to bounce back strongly in 2027.
"He will recover," said Wolff. "I have no doubt about that for next year.
"And all the very best sports people have gone through difficult periods and that's going to be a part of his continued development."
Russell's hitherto best F1 championship finish is fourth, which he achieved in 2022 and 2025.
'2027 season has started now' - Wolff says next season won't be easy for Mercedes

While Mercedes have become world champions again with room to spare this year, the early-season dominance that laid the significant groundwork for their title triumphs in the first season of the sport's latest ruleset appears a long time ago now.
Antonelli's win at the United States Grand Prix last month is their only victory in the last five races amid ever-increasing competitiveness between the grid's four teams at the front of the field.
Wolff believes all three of Mercedes chief rivals will be in next year's world title fight.
"Look at the last few races, we haven't won," said Wolff.

"At the beginning of the race [in Brazil], Kimi was just storming away, it looked like this could be ours. But the competition has been getting tougher between Ferrari, McLaren, Red Bull and ourselves.
"It's four teams that can win races and will be challenging for a world championship.
"And I have no doubt that it's going to be very difficult for us next year. For me, the 2027 season has started now.

"It is about learning in the three last races. What is it we can optimise? What didn't we spot when we put the upgrade on the car? What is it we can learn from [race day in Brazil] and attack these last three races full blast, while also making sure that we have the learning for next year's power unit and next year's car?"

articles.title: Mahomes has a new star and Cousins fights back tears - NFL Sunday Review

paras.en: NFL: Patrick Mahomes has a new star, Kirk Cousins' emotional story continues and Christian McCaffrey lights up the Dallas Cowboys - NFL Sunday Review

NFL Sunday Review - we reflect on Week 10 in the NFL as Emmett Johnson announced himself as a new star on the Kansas City Chiefs, Kirk Cousins capped a memorable return for the Minnesota Vikings and Christian McCaffrey dominated in the San Francisco 49ers' win over the Dallas Cowboys.

"There's more of the story to be written." Kirk Cousins could barely fight back the tears as he processed a day he thought might never come, a second chance he thought might never arrive. But football can't keep Kirko Chainz down, and suddenly the Minnesota Vikings have hope.

It is the easiest story in the NFL to get behind. A 38-year-old Kirk Cousins, written off more times than he can count, deemed deep into the back nine of his career, coming back to a hero's welcome to spearhead a playoff charge while lighting a fire under an offense in desperate need of inspiration. His inspiration.

He is football's lovable goof, with the unpretentious, unflashy dad clothes and a 'down with the kids' willingness to sling on Justin Jefferson's chains should it lift his teammates. He is also now Minnesota's great hope of rewarding defensive mastery with an attack capable of competing in January football.
The Vikings were limping behind Kyler Murray, limping behind Carson Wentz but sitting a coveted 6-2, and on Tuesday rolled the dice by trading to bring back Cousins from the Las Vegas Raiders.

It was three years ago that Cousins played the final game of his first chapter with the Vikings when he tore his Achilles tendon in Week Eight against the Green Bay Packers at Lambeau Field. On Sunday he was back where it ended - but could it yet be where it all started again?

Cousins, who had revived his starting career as mentor to No 1 pick Mendoza in Las Vegas, finished 21 of 31 for 207 yards, two touchdowns and one interception in his first game back as the Vikings stunned the Packers 30-10.

His start featured a perfectly placed sideline strike between two defenders to a reception-starved Justin Jefferson on third-and-second in the first quarter, and so too a high-level tight-window bullet to Myles Price for a 38-yard touchdown catch-and-run on third-and-23.

It would become Jefferson's best game of the season as he made eight catches from nine targets for 92 yards and two touchdowns, Cousins' reconnecting with one of the stars of the league having seen him suffer for the first half of the season.

Much of the debate and, at times, criticism around Cousins throughout his career has been the shortage of point guard ability as a needle-moving creator. The Patrick Mahomes' and Josh Allens and Joe Burrows and Lamar Jacksons of the world have unfortunately heightened that bar for all quarterbacks across the league. But what has never been in doubt with Cousins is the efficiency at which he feeds his best players, and at which he moves the ball and at which he can accentuate an offense's strengths without being spectacular. Spectacular isn't exactly needed when there is a Brian Flores defense foaming at the mouth in wait of their chance to go hunting on the sideline.

paras.en: In one game the Vikings looked a more polished, more accomplished operation behind Cousins, and alongside that came another rampant defensive play that saw Minnesota sack Jordan Love eight times.

In the first half alone they produced five sacks, 12 pressures, one interception and one fumble recovery, including sacks on back-to-back plays at the end of the second quarter. Their sixth sack then arrived on the very first play from scrimmage after the break, followed by the third of their four turnovers when Dallas Turner recover a wayward snap.

They were frightening, and the perfect complement once Cousins had helped the Vikings get on top early. The impact was evidenced through the time of possession, Cousins' offense holding the ball for 17.55 minutes in the first half and 35.16 a week on since the Vikings mustered just 17 minutes and 28 seconds of possession against the Bills. What a difference some respite for one of the league's most potent defenses makes.

There was a nice moment in the second half when former New Orleans Saints quarterback Drew Brees paid tribute to Cousins' communication at the line of scrimmage, where he shifted personnel and changed the play like an orchestra conductor. It was long-lost control and assurance under center.

Cousins later executed a trick play that saw him pump fake left and the swivel to pump fake to his right before tossing to Gavin Bartholomew over the middle of the field for a touchdown. For Kevin O'Connell to dial up a play like that just days after Cousins' arrival is testament to the footballing brain now leading Minnesota's offense.

"It was emotional coming to this stadium three years ago, tearing my Achilles here. It's been a tough three years, just grateful for the opportunity to play here, grateful for my teammates and what they did to make this outcome possible.
"It's been a tough three years. There's more of the story to be written," said Cousins post-game, his voice cracking several times."

Cousins won just one playoff game in six seasons during his first stint with the Vikings, before signing a four-year $180m contract with the Atlanta Falcons in 2024, only to be bench for Michael Penix Jr in his first season. He was then released in March earlier this year before landing in Las Vegas as something of a bridge towards their new era under Mendoza.
What looked like a declining career hurtling towards its end is instead flirting with one final twist.

Patrick Mahomes' new friends are alright. The Kansas City Chiefs were without their best player this season in Kenneth Walker III on Sunday; it did not matter. The absence of last season's Super Bowl MVP paved the way for an increased role for fifth-round rookie running back Emmett Johnson, who capitalised emphatically with 22 carries for 101 yards and six catches for 70 yards and two scores through the air as Kansas City beat the Atlanta Falcons 35-13 in a five-touchdown day for Patrick Mahomes. Johnson showcased his menu of evasive manoeuvres in the open field with a clinic in tackle-missing jukes and the yards-after-catch threat primed to see him become one of Andy Reid's favourite weapons over the second half of the season.

paras.en: There was also a debut for wide receiver Josh Downs, who had four catches for 53 yards and a touchdown in his first game since arriving via a trade from the Indianapolis Colts. It's been a long time since Mahomes and the Chiefs posed a consistent vertical threat but Downs could prove an answer to as much. Mahomes completed seven of 12 attempts on passes of 10-plus air yards for 206 yards and three touchdowns, while going three of six on attempts of 20-plus yards for 132 yards and two scores. The Chiefs offense is clicking.

paras.en: Denzel Ward is playing at an All-Pro level. It is hard to be one of the best players on the league for so long on a team that has been bad for so long; Myles Garrett did it in Cleveland, and Denzel Ward is still doing it. He stepped up when the Browns needed him most on Sunday with a stunning diving pass break-up against Xavier Hutchinson to deny the Houston Texans with 30 seconds left in Cleveland's 27-24 victory. Ward allowed just four receptions for 16 yards from nine targets on Sunday while lining up against Nico Collins in man coverage on 10 of 11 routes, according to Next Gen Stats. Pat Surtain II may still hold the honour of top dog in the eyes of many, but Ward will feel he holds a strong argument as being the best corner in football.

paras.en: There are encouraging signs for Fernando Mendoza. The Raiders ushered in a new chapter this weekend as No 1 overall Draft pick Mendoza led his side out against the Seattle Seahawks in his first regular season start following Cousins' trade to the Vikings. It started strongly with a touchdown run on his opening possession before Mike Macdonald dialled the pressure up a notch on defense in the second half as the Raiders offense suffered without star weapon Brock Bowers. He went 11 of 13 for 90 yards through the air in the first half, before managing just six of 16 for 53 yards following the interval. Mendoza finished the game 17 of 29 passing for 143 yards, zero touchdowns and zero turnovers while being sacked six times. Facing the league's best defense always beckoned as a baptism of fire, so the shortage of interceptions or apparent ball security issues was a plus point.

paras.en: Brock Purdy is a top five quarterback in the NFL. For somebody so often pigeonholed as a 'system quarterback', he sure does do a lot of good outside of the system. Purdy continues to showcase an elite ability to extend plays and create outside of the pocket, perhaps best epitomised by the 74-yard McCaffrey touchdown catch-and-run that saw him side-step a near-certain sack, slide to his left, cut back inside and fire a dart to his open running back. Poise in the face of chaos and a ground threat that makes him dangerous off-script. Purdy finished the game 22 of 28 for 389 yards and three touchdowns with a 154.5 passer rating. He is in the MVP hunt and playing at a level among the premier play-callers in football. By now, though, he knows his true judgement comes around playoff time.

McCaffrey went off for 223 scrimmage yards and three touchdowns to tear apart of hobbling Cowboys defense, which surrendered a franchise-worst 584 yards at home. McCaffrey's 161 receiving yards were the most by a running back in a game since Jamaal Charles' 195 in 2013, while he is the first 49ers player with 200 scrimmage yards and three scores in a regular season game since Jerry Rice in 1995.

Jahmyr Gibbs is a familiar resident in this slot, but he is impossible to ignore as the clear frontrunner for Offensive Player of the Year through 10 weeks. The Lions running back was at his scintillating best in Munich as he put up 252 scrimmage yards and two touchdowns to torch the Patriots defense, his 62 career touchdowns breaking Terrell Davis' record for most by a player through his first four seasons in NFL history. He is not only the perfect cocktail of speed and shiftiness, but one of the smartest crease detectors in football. He runs hard, he runs fast, he runs with high-powered intelligence as the focal point of Drew Petzing's Lions offense. Another clinic, this time on European soil, to extend his lead as the NFL leader in scrimmage yards.

articles.title: Trump, Xi and Putin plan an unprecedented  meeting on the sidelines of APEC, officials say
articles.author: Caroline Kenny

paras.en: President Donald Trump will meet with the leaders of China and Russia on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzen, China’s tech hub, next week, an unprecedented gathering of the heads of the world’s biggest nuclear powers.

“President Trump will conclude his visit to China with a trilateral meeting between the president of the United States, the president of the People’s Republic of China and the president of the Russian Federation,” Olivia Wales, a White House spokesperson, said in a call with reporters Friday night. “The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous.”

It is not anticipated that any sort of agreement will come from the trilateral meeting, according to a senior U.S. official, who described the session as an “entry point” and “the first conversation,” pointing to the reduction of nuclear arsenals as a key topic.

“We do think it’s time for China to sort of step up, you know, to the adults’ table, if you will, and have adult conversations about adult things,” the senior U.S. official said about the issue of nuclear weapons.

Beijing’s arsenal of more than 600 warheads, according to Pentagon estimates, is far smaller than inventories held by the U.S. and Russia, each estimated to have more than 5,000 warheads. With U.S. and Russian arsenals dwarfing its stockpile, China has shown little interest in developing a nuclear pact.

The last nuclear arms pact between Russia and the United States expired in February, removing caps on the two largest atomic arsenals for the first time in more than a half-century. When that treaty — known as New START — expired, Trump rejected a call by Russia to extend the two-country deal for another year and called for “a new, improved and modernized” deal that includes China.
The three-way summit with Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin comes at a complicated moment in relations for the three countries.

Trump intends to discuss the Iran war with the two leaders, but not the war in Ukraine, according to a senior U.S. official, who noted that discussions about the war in Ukraine are a separate “track” that China is not part of so it would not be “appropriate.”

Trump has warmly embraced Xi after coming to a truce in their short-lived trade war last year and in spite of differences over the U.S. war with Iran and other tensions between the world’s foremost economic powers.

Similarly, Trump has sought to build his relationship with Putin, even as the Russian leader has persisted in his nearly 5-year-old war with Ukraine and as Moscow has deepened its military, intelligence and diplomatic partnership with Iran.
There is no bilateral with Putin scheduled, but the two leaders will appear at events and the trilateral meeting together, according to a senior U.S. official.
There are no plans for Trump to engage with North Korea during the trip, according to a senior U.S. official.

Separately, Elon Musk will be the only business leader who is part of the president’s delegation, according to a senior U.S. official, who noted that other U.S. business leaders will attend the summit in their own capacity but there is no official U.S. business delegation.
Musk will not be part of any official meetings, according to a senior U.S. official.

Two senior U.S. officials said that they don’t think Trump will raise the espionage investigation focused on Alice Huang, an alleged Chinese intelligence agent who allegedly had a romantic relationship with Nvidia chief Jensen Huang, with China.

“The situation with Nvidia should not really have any bearing on the trip. In all of our discussions and negotiations with the Chinese, we do not negotiate American export controls,” a senior U.S. official said. “These are national security matters that we develop in the administration and interagency process, and we don’t expect it to figure at all in any of our conversations with the Chinese while we’re there.”
Beijing was least certain about the value of the summit
By agreeing to host the meeting, Xi may be calculating that the moment offers him an opportunity to flex China’s growing clout and prestige.
For the Kremlin, the planned trilateral meeting is a coveted chance to posture as a superpower on par with Washington and Beijing.

“I think the key for Putin was that this was very much about signaling a desire to talk to the president and talk to Chairman Xi in a way that suggests that they’re making decisions on Ukraine, which obviously the Ukrainians and the Europeans don’t like,” said Edgard Kagan, a former U.S. ambassador to Malaysia who is now at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

The trilateral could very well overshadow the APEC summit. The summit, which is bringing 21 economies to Shenzhen, marks a big moment for China to show off its fast-growing, ultramodern coastal metropolis that transformed from a small fishing village into a global technology and economic hub in just a few decades.

More substantively, such a gathering could also muddy China’s argument that a Cold War mentality in the West was a contributing factor that led to Russia’s war on Ukraine and its pointed criticism that the U.S. has undermined international institutions and treaties with how it has executed its war against Iran.

The trilateral meeting could undercut China’s push to portray itself as a defender of free trade at APEC, said Hoo Tiang Boon, a professor of Chinese foreign policy at Nanyang Technological University.
“You sort of run counter to Chinese support of multilateralism,” he said.
The leaders have met in pairs plenty of times over the years
Putin and Xi are no strangers. They’ve fostered a close personal relationship, meeting more than 40 times since Xi became president in 2013 and addressing each other as “dear friend.”

Trump and Putin have met face-to-face on seven different occasions, most recently in Alaska in August 2025. Xi and Trump have held face-to-face talks on eight occasions, including a September state visit to Washington by Xi.
Beijing is the No. 1 trading partner for Moscow, a relationship that has strengthened since Putin sent troops into Ukraine in 2022.

As the EU and the West sought to economically isolate Russia, China increased its purchases of Russia’s energy resources and became Moscow’s principal supplier of key technologies, including high-tech components for Russian weapons industries. Beijing has ignored Western demands to cut those supplies.

In the lead-up to Russia’s war on Ukraine, Xi and Putin declared their countries had a “no-limits friendship.” China officially has said it is neutral on the conflict, while charging that Kyiv’s Western allies played a part in provoking Russia’s military action in Ukraine.
Moscow, in turn, has repeatedly declared its support for Beijing’s policy on issues related to Taiwan.

Trump recently struck a diesel deal with Russia, waiving sanctions against Moscow and allowing for the sale of millions of tons of the fuel. The U.S. leader has blamed surging energy prices on Ukraine’s attacks on Russian oil refineries. Analysts, however, say the rise in global crude prices is due mostly to the Iran war.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has expressed concern that the trilateral meeting could serve as a platform for discussing a possible Ukraine deal behind Kyiv’s back.

Planning for the summit has drawn comparisons to the Yalta Conference, the 1945 gathering at which the leaders of the U.S., Britain and the Soviet Union agreed to divide Germany and Berlin into four military occupation zones and finalized plans for establishing the United Nations.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has dismissed the Yalta comparisons, noting that any potential agreements reached in Shenzhen can’t be enforced on others.

“It’s clear that a meeting between the leaders of countries such as Russia, China and the United States is extremely significant,” Peskov said. “However, let’s not forget that the vision for a global order is that no one tries to impose any particular view of global order, and it should be based entirely on mutual benefit and mutual respect.”

articles.title: Small regional town fights back against proposed AI data centre
articles.author: Charlotte Wilkes and Steve Martin

paras.en: Thousands of Victorians protested against data centres on Saturday including dozens from the small town of Miners Rest.
Miners Rest, north of Ballarat, is home to just under 4,000 people and is the proposed location for a data centre to be constructed by Resi Ventures.
Protesters are calling for a statewide moratorium on the construction of AI data centres.
The small regional town of Miners Rest, north of Ballarat, is home to just under 4,000 people.

Locals say their quiet country life might be about to change after developer Resi Ventures announced to the Australian Stock Exchange in June its intention to build an AI data centre at the town's old quarry.
Volunteer firefighter and First Nations man Jedd Willis said the proposal on a 67 hectare plot of land in his town had been overwhelming.
"There been a complete lack of care for country which disturbs me as a First Nations person," Mr Willis said.
"[The site] has a very valuable resource for water and for firefighting."
Mr Willis, who is a CFA volunteer, said firefighters would often use the water at the proposed site for fighting bushfires.
"Without that [water] source, we'd be forced to rely more heavily on the treatment plant,"

"Along that, the concerns around the lack of water availability across the state as a whole, let alone just this region and with the upcoming fire season being forecasted to be quite treacherous is concerning."
On Saturday, dozens of Miners Rest locals joined thousands from across the state at the steps of the state library in Melbourne to protest against the rise of AI data centres in Victoria.
As of September this year, there were 50 data centres operating across Victoria with another 18 in the pipeline.
Protesters called for a statewide moratorium on their construction.
Secretary for the No Data Centre Miners Rest group, Chris Phillips said the developer had not been open about its plans.
He said locals learned about this proposal through the media, rather than consultation with the community.
"It's been extremely difficult [to find information about it],"
"The benefit to the community would be very little."
Mr Phillips said one of his concerns was whether the company would be making use of an aquifer at the site.
"There's an aquifer [at the site] that goes many hundreds of kilometres underground and people draw water out of that to grow food like, potato farmers," he said.
"We're scared that water could get contaminated and flow through to the rest of our agricultural industry and be a blight on our area."
Mr Phillips said locals were also concerned about the noise pollution that could come from the centre.
"It's going to have a noise transmission of 63 to 65 decibels, which will be heard up to 1 kilometre away, over a constant 24 hours," he said.
He said he would be anxiously watching the upcoming election and hoped politicians were listening to the local community.
"I think if [politicians] don't listen to people they're going to get a very, very rude shock come this election," he said.
"We are very nervously watching and we've had commitments from various political parties but we are also very nervous as to what could happen once the party is elected we could be steam rolled."
In a statement Ripon MP, Martha Haylett said Miners Rest families deserved to be consulted before decisions were made that could fundamentally change their local area.
"There has been no planning approval, no permits issued, and no meaningful consultation with the community," Ms Haylett said.
"A project of this scale and significance cannot be imposed on a community without proper scrutiny, transparency, and engagement."
The City of Ballarat said in a statement it had not received any planning applications for the proposal.
"While Council officers have had early conversations with the developer, no formal applications have been lodged," it said.
"All planning applications are subject to a thorough assessment process."
The ABC has contacted Resi Ventures for comment.
