articles.title: Carney sets out to deepen ties with China. Has the threat landscape changed?
articles.author: Racy Rafique

paras.en: Carney sets out to deepen ties with China. Has the threat landscape changed?
PM says he will raise concerns about foreign interference in meeting with Xi Jinping
On the sidelines of the APEC summit this coming week, Prime Minister Mark Carney is set to meet with his Chinese counterpart, President Xi Jinping, in hopes of deepening economic and trade ties.
It's the second meeting between the two leaders in less than a year, and this time it will take place in Shenzen, China, where the summit is being held on Wednesday and Thursday.
While Carney has been working to rebuild Canada's economic and trade relationship with China, experts warn that it doesn't mean the threat to Canada has weakened.

Canada's relationship with China might have improved, but the "serious national and economic security threats to Canada ... have not fundamentally changed," said Vina Nadjibulla, co-founder and CEO of the Centre for Strategic Statecraft, a new non-partisan think-tank with offices in Vancouver and Ottawa.

"What has changed is not China's behaviour but Canada's strategic circumstances and the Carney government's approach," she told CBC News. "With growing uncertainty in our relationship with the United States, there are compelling reasons to stabilize relations with Beijing, pursue economic opportunities and diversify our trade."

In an interview on Rosemary Barton Live that aired Sunday, Jody Thomas, national security adviser to Justin Trudeau when he was prime minister, echoed Nadjibulla's views, adding that "the prime minister is pursuing an economic relationship, I hope, and I think with the understanding of the national security threat posed by China."

Speaking to reporters in Montreal on Tuesday, Carney said he will raise concerns about foreign interference in Canada, adding, "The advantage of these meetings is you can raise issues directly and frankly."
Carney said he would be bringing up the importance that Canada attaches "to the non-interference in our affairs by China and other countries."
The economic and trade relationship between Canada and China "is something that is deepening but has clear guardrails in terms of the areas in which we're involved," he said.

It's hard to talk about national security threats from China without pointing to the much-publicized affair between Jensen Huang, who resigned on Thursday as CEO of chip-making giant Nvidia, and an alleged Chinese spy.

For Nvidia, the turmoil over the sex-and-spy scandal and Huang's resignation have cost in excess of $1 trillion US in market value. The political ramifications for U.S. President Donald Trump and his administration remain to be seen.
- The Nvidia scandal has wiped away $1T in value. What that means for your investments
- How China gets around the U.S. ban on Nvidia chips

"What I hope doesn't get lost in all of this is the incredible vulnerability of this kind of concentration in our industry, in our economy and in our politics," former U.S. trade representative Katherine Tai told CBC News chief political correspondent Rosemary Barton.

"How vulnerable you become when you are so reliant on one company that makes one particular product that is apparently there to prop up the major growth industry in your economy. We here in the United States find ourselves in an incredibly precarious place."
Carney shared a similar observation at Tuesday's news conference in Montreal.
Referring to China, Carney said, "In terms of the security risks of our partnership, they are much, much, much less than the security risks, for example, [faced by] the United States."
But Nadjibulla said the situation is a bit more nuanced than that.
Vina Nadjibulla, co-founder and CEO of the Centre for Strategic Statecraft, a new non-partisan think-tank, is shown in Ottawa in June 2023. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)
While the U.S. and China are "peer competitors" engaged in a global struggle for economic, technological and military leadership, Canada is in a fundamentally different position, she said.

"We are a much smaller, more open economy, with considerably less leverage in dealing with Beijing. That makes us more vulnerable to certain forms of economic coercion and political pressure, not less."

But even then, the question is not whether Canada faces the same level of risk as the U.S., Nadjibulla said. The question is whether Canada has the tools and capacity to manage the risks it does face.

Former national security adviser Jody Thomas points to Canada's own recent experience with alleged Chinese spying: the Canadian NATO intern who was arrested in July on charges of espionage allegedly tied to China.
Thomas said that incident and the Nvidia situation shed light on how China operates — but also how Canada needs to adapt to potential threats in the artificial intelligence space.

"What I think it means for Canada is that the approach the prime minister is taking with having a minister responsible for AI, setting up the [National Council on Artificial Intelligence], advising in terms of how to use that AI, how to regulate AI and how to ensure that the safety guardrails are developed."

articles.title: Steering issue caused tanker to crash into cruise boat, U.S. officials say

paras.en: Steering issue caused tanker to crash into cruise boat, U.S. officials say
National Transportation Safety Board says cause of problem not yet known

The asphalt tanker vessel that struck a docked paddlewheel cruise boat in the Mississippi River at New Orleans on Friday experienced a steering problem in which its rudder was stuck in one position, U.S. transportation safety officials said on Sunday.
The American Cruise Lines passenger vessel American Heritage, with 190 people aboard, capsized at the dock, but no one was killed in the collision.

The Atlantic Asphalt tanker was headed upriver when it experienced a "steering casualty" in which its rudder stayed in a starboard position and the vessel veered toward the river's east bank, U.S. National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) senior marine accident investigator Bart Barnum told a news conference in New Orleans.
NTSB officials said they do not know what caused the steering problem. The tanker's voyage data recorder was recovered on Saturday.

Issues under investigation include whether the tanker's anchors were deployed and, if so, at what depth, as well as interviews with crew members and passengers, officials said. Interviews with the crew of the Atlantic Asphalt are scheduled over the next week, they said.
Harbour personnel, firefighters and onlookers scrambled to pull passengers from the cruise vessel to safety after the collision. The cruise vessel toppled over into the river.

articles.title: 'I cheated': South Korean admits he used AI to achieve top score in national exam

paras.en: 'I cheated': South Korean admits he used AI to achieve top score in national exam
Revelation prompts 'countermeasures' from officials ahead of college entrance exams

The marks attained by the top scorer on South Korea's national exam for aspiring tax accountants this year seemed too good to be true, and on Sunday, skeptics were proven right when he confessed to using generative AI to cheat.

The scandal follows months of speculation after he scored near-perfect marks on hundreds of questions over two exams taken in April and July. It has also raised the stakes for organizers of South Korea's high-stakes annual college entrance exam this Thursday.

"I cheated using electronic devices and generative AI. My passing the exam with the top score was not the result of fair effort," he said, identifying himself by the surname Han, as he apologized on the YouTube channel Attorney Lee Don-ho.
Han said he cheated by taking photos of the exam questions with a microcamera, sending them to an artificial intelligence tool and checking the answers on a smartphone.
Speaking on camera wearing a face mask, Han added that he had submitted a written confession to Seoul police.
A Reuters call to the Seoul Jungbu police station went unanswered on Sunday.
The scandal has rattled a country where standardized tests largely dictate social mobility and career trajectories, coming just four days ahead of Thursday's annual national college entrance exam.

"The presidential office views the matter very seriously, and because the college entrance exam is next week, we have been working hard to prepare countermeasures," a senior presidential office official told reporters on Sunday.

The official said that reports of potential cheating in the certified public accountant exam were concerning, adding that the presidential chief of staff for policy would convene an emergency meeting later in the afternoon to address the issue.
Students wait for the start of the annual college entrance examinations in a Seoul classroom in November 2025. (Kim Hong-ji/The Associated Press)

Prime Minister Han Seong-sook acknowledged on Friday public concerns over AI-assisted cheating ahead of the national college entrance exam, a high-pressure event that many South Korean students have spent much of their lives preparing for.

The government "will prepare thoroughly in advance and closely oversee the process until the very end to ensure the college entrance exam is conducted fairly and stably," a statement from her office said.

articles.title: Gen Z protests: Do Baby Boomers really have it better than young people?

paras.en: Young people across Germany and Europe are taking to the streets, voicing fears of a bleak future.
But is that really the case? Does Gen Z face greater challenges than Baby Boomers did in the 1990s? What do the two generations have in common, and where do their experiences differ?

"Of course, it's fair to ask, 'Were things just as tough for you back then?'" youth researcher Simon Schnetzer tells DW. "But young people see that things are difficult for them now, and say that's why they need support today."

Schnetzer, who wrote the annual Youth in Germany study, highlights one key question raised by the recent demonstrations across Europe as: "Have we given young people the conditions they need to live and work here with confidence, and to keep this system funded?"

His straightforward answer is no. A survey of the statistics shows that both Gen Z and the Baby Boomers are affected by major societal changes, but in different ways. DW surveyed data on pensions, education, housing and climate change to find out more.

The facts point to a clear trend: Fewer and fewer young people are having to support an ever-growing number of retirees. According to the Germany's public pension insurance system, there were 3.73 contributors for every retiree in 1957. By 2025, that figure had fallen to just 2.1.
By 2045, this number is projected to drop to just 1.73 contributors per retiree. In absolute terms, this means 35.35 million contributors will be financing pensions for 16.82 million retirees.

To cushion this trend and keep contribution rates stable, the pension system already receives around €118 billion [$131 billion] in annual government subsidies. This amounts to roughly 25% of the federal budget. That means an increasing share of the population will be called upon to help fund pensions.

There are also signs that many people's pensions are already falling short of covering their living expenses. The number of retirees relying on federal basic income support has risen from 257,000 in 2003 to 738,000 in 2024.

Rising rents hit low-income households particularly hard. According to a report by the German Institute for Economic Research (DIW), the share of income spent on rent by low-income households rose from around 24% in 1990 to nearly 36% in 2021.
This means that in 2021, the lowest-income households spent an average of 14 percentage points more of their income on rent than high-income households.

According to Germany's Federal Statistical Office (Destatis), in 2025, an average of 11% of the population spent more than 40% of their disposable income on housing costs. Among people at risk of poverty, the figure was as high as 35%.

However, according to calculations by real estate platform Jacasa, Boomers could actually help ease pressure on the housing market in the coming years. They currently own around 4.8 million owner-occupied houses and apartments.

Over the coming decades, these properties are expected to change hands as former occupants sell them, move into assisted living, or hand them down through inheritance. In some regions, this could lead to an oversupply of properties and, consequently, lower prices, according to Jacasa's projections.

According to the federal government's Education Finance Report, public spending on education for people under 30 has doubled since 2011, rising from around €4,000 to approximately €8,000 per person annually.

Despite this increase, Germany ranks only in the middle of the pack internationally. According to the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis), public education spending accounted for 4.6% of Germany's gross domestic product (GDP) in 2022, compared with an OECD average of 4.7%.

However, the additional funding cannot solve the problem of teacher shortages. According to estimates by the Standing Conference of the Ministers of Education and Cultural Affairs, Germany will be short of around 27,000 teachers by 2035. The main reasons are the wave of Baby Boomer retirements and declining birth rates, which have contributed to a shortage of young teachers.

Back in 1972, the Club of Rome warned of the consequences of global warming in its landmark publication The Limits to Growth. According to the United Nations, the planet is on track for 2.6°C of warming by the end of the century compared with pre-industrial levels.

If the world maintains its current climate policies, children who are six years old today could experience heat waves two to seven times as often as Boomers did over their lifetimes. That was the finding of a 2025 study by Vrije University in Brussels.

The deadly impact of extreme weather is already evident in rising death tolls during recent heatwaves. According to Germany's Robert Koch Institute (RKI), an estimated 16,000 people died from heat-related causes across Germany by mid-September 2026. The vast majority — more than 14,000 — were over the age of 65.

"Gen Z and Baby Boomers are in the same boat. We need to bring them together, because otherwise younger people have no prospects for prosperity, and neither do older generations," youth researcher Schnetzer concludes.

He suggests that both generations take to the streets and protest together, adding that would just be the beginning. "What needs to follow is a constructive process to define goals and measures that everyone can support," he said. "Even if it means making sacrifices."
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Turkey uses espionage accusations to pressure government critics

paras.en: When police officers appeared at her home in Istanbul last Wednesday evening, Yonca Verdioglu Sik was surprised — even more so when they took her in for questioning. Her lawyer says she was accused of political and military espionage.

But, according to transcripts of the interrogation that were published later, Verdioglu Sik was never asked any questions about espionage. Instead the public prosecutor's office appeared to be more interested in the activities of her German employer, the Heinrich Böll Foundation.

For 18 years, Verdioglu Sik, who was born and raised in Germany, has been the foundation's project coordinator. In her role, she organizes projects that focus on democracy and the rights of women, minorities and LGBTQ+ people.
During the interrogation, transfers of money from the foundation into her bank account were discussed. Verdioglu Sik found out that she was now also subject to a travel ban.

Verdioglu Sik was eventually released, but her arrest caused outrage among critics of the Turkish government. She is married to investigative journalist and member of parliament, Ahmet Sik. He belongs to the left-wing Workers' Party of Turkey, or TIP, and is known as one of the harshest critics of the current government.

Sik has recently been looking into a stock market scandal, which allegedly benefited members of the ruling Justice and Development Party, or AKP, headed by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, and associates.
Opposition critics drew a clear conclusion: As a member of parliament, Sik has parliamentary immunity. So instead, the justice system is putting pressure on him through his wife.
"If you take away a state's law, what is left is no longer called a state, but a gang," Sik responded to the arrest in writing.

Verdioglu Sik's arrest is not the first such case in Turkey. Ever since the attempted coup against the Erdogan government in 2016, accusations of espionage have been leveled at a wide variety of groups in Turkey: journalists, opposition figures and human rights activists as well as employees of foreign embassies and staff of foreign institutions like nongovernmental organizations and foundations.

Such accusations have often been followed by acquittals or convictions for other offenses, albeit sometimes years later. But what the many instances have in common is what's known as a "chilling effect." Any investigation can mean lengthy pre-trial detention, reputational and professional damage and even social isolation.
In the past, such cases have even triggered diplomatic spats.

In 2015, for example, Can Dundar and Erdem Gul, both senior journalists at the opposition daily Cumhuriyet, were accused of espionage after reporting that Turkey had tried to ship arms to rebels fighting the Syrian government. Dundar now lives in exile in Berlin.
In 2017, Erdogan said that reporter Deniz Yücel, then working for German newspaper Die Welt, was a "German agent." That led to a serious diplomatic crisis between Berlin and Ankara.

Espionage charges have also been laid against local employees of the US diplomatic corps and against a lawyer working for the German embassy. US pastor Andrew Brunson and his wife were also arrested because of alleged links to Kurdish anti-government groups. Turkish philanthropist and human rights activist Osman Kavala, who was charged with espionage and attempting to overthrow the constitutional order, remains in prison.
Most recently, espionage charges have been brought against the former Istanbul mayor and Erdogan's political competitor, Ekrem Imamoglu, and a number of journalists.
Hakki Tas, a research fellow and expert on Turkey at the German Institute for Global and Area Studies, said the number of such cases have been increasing over the past few years.

On the one hand, Turkey has the right to protect itself from foreign intelligence services — especially given geopolitical competition and conflict in the region, he argued. On the other hand, there's a long tradition of bringing the Turkish opposition to court to face security charges.
"What foreigners or employees of foreign institutions have experienced in recent years is a continuation of this pattern," Tas told DW.

Media outlets and NGOs critical of the government have faced investigations, trials and other sorts of state sanctions for years. The ruling AKP party has also brought in its own version of a so-called "foreign agent law."
These sorts of espionage cases serve both a domestic and foreign policy function, Tas said.

For locals, "contact with a foreign institution, foreign funding or even a perfectly normal salary could become part of an investigation someday," he explained. "For opposition figures and civil society organizations, in particular, this can become a security issue."

In terms of foreign policy, the cases also show other countries that there are limits to their activities inside Turkey. These kinds of accusations seem to become more frequent when there's some sort of foreign policy tension — for example, after Western criticism of how opposition groups were dealt with after the alleged coup in 2016, the aforementioned disputes about arms deliveries in connection with Syria, or criticism from abroad about the removal of elected mayors in Turkey.
It can also serve as a kind of "hostage diplomacy," Tas said.

The case of US pastor Brunson is a good example. After his arrest, the Turkish government proposed a trade with the Americans. They wanted to exchange Turkish preacher Fethullah Gulen, who lived in the US and who the Turkish government blamed for the 2016 coup attempt.

This suspicion of foreign institutions isn't something that the Erdogan government invented, Tas points out. In the early 2000s, several representatives of German organizations were already made to stand trial in Turkey. At the time, it was alleged that, among other things, the German spy service was using German foundations as a front for conspiracy.

In some of the best-known cases, defendants often don't end up convicted of espionage. In the case of activist Osman Kavala, he was initially acquitted of espionage several times and spent two years in prison, just because of those charges.
But Tas said that's no surprise, referring to a 1979 work about the sociology of law written by US law professor Malcolm Feeley. It's title: "The Process Is the Punishment."
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Goodbye, overtourism? Sustainable travel gains ground

paras.en: Latin America is currently one of the world's most dynamic tourism regions. According to UN Tourism, the United Nations agency responsible for promoting responsible tourism, international arrivals in South America grew by 7% last year, while Central America saw a 5% increase, both above the global average.

But the boom comes at a price: overtourism. In some destinations, the sheer number of visitors is creating environmental and social problems, fueling tensions and raising questions about who really benefits from the business.

One famous example is Machu Picchu, the Inca citadel in Peru, which lures up to 5,600 visitors a day. In 2025, Peru's official watchdog warned that more tickets were being sold than permitted, potentially putting the site at risk of being added to UNESCO's List of World Heritage in Danger. The UNESCO World Heritage Committee has already expressed its concern.

In a bid to protect the Galapagos Islands and its bountiful ecosystems that inspired Charles Darwin, Ecuador doubled the entrance fee for foreign visitors to $200 in 2024. Even so, pressure is mounting to construct new hotels and tourist apartments. And in Mexico City, the influx of tourists and digital nomads into neighborhoods such as Roma and Condesa has fueled protests over rising rents.

What can be done to make tourism more inclusive and sustainable? That's one of the industry's biggest questions. At ITB Americas, an international travel trade fair in Guadalajara, Mexico, DW spoke with three experts.
Sustainable travel moving from niche to mainstream

Richard Bazan is a regional manager for the Americas at Planeterra, a nonprofit organization that promotes and supports community-based tourism. He said several trends are emerging: group sizes are shrinking and travelers are seeking more intimate experiences.
"Where groups of 20 used to travel together, now it's four or five," he told DW.

So-called "nature-positive" tourism is also gaining traction, with travel programs that help fund, for example, reforestation projects. Bazan said even all-inclusive resorts are realizing that they can no longer shut themselves off from their surroundings. Instead, they need to offer authentic experiences that connect visitors with the destination.
"Community-based tourism is no longer a niche," he said.

Pressure for change is also coming from travelers themselves. According to Booking.com's 2025 annual survey, which polled 32,000 people in 34 countries, 93% said they wanted to make more sustainable travel choices. For the first time, more than half (53%) were aware of tourism's impact on local communities, not just the environment.
Communities know what's best for their land

Sarah Payne, director of the Reset Tourism Fund at the UnTours Foundation, pointed to the underlying problem. In the traditional tourism business model, most of the money generated never reaches local communities, the people who actually live with the influx of visitors.

"Access to financing is key, yet extremely difficult for communities," she explained. The financial products on the market tend to be expensive and inflexible, as tourism is considered a high-risk sector. Her foundation's fund offers low-interest loans with flexible repayment terms. Its guiding principle is that communities generally know what's best for their own land.

Sebastian Munoz, co-founder of Rutopia, a platform specializing in ecotourism and community-based tourism, has brought his experience from the nonprofit sector into social enterprise. His believes tours must be designed in partnership with communities so they feel a sense of ownership, rather than seeing them as something imposed from outside.

Bazan, meanwhile, thinks community-based tourism should not be approached as a humanitarian project, but through a market-driven lens: understanding what visitors are looking for and then planning hand-in-hand with the local community. In other words, building bridges between these two distinct worlds.
"It's not sustainable to create a product if no one comes to experience it," he said.

The big question is how to grow without sacrificing sustainability. For Bazan, that decision doesn't belong to the tourism industry. Communities themselves must decide how they want to grow, and outside players should not pressure them. Their role, he said, is to amplify local voices, not to bring solutions or investments. "We have to learn to listen," he said.

The impact of community-based tourism is difficult to measure, Munoz acknowledged, because it has social impacts that go beyond the numbers. He cited the example of the Indigenous Mixtec community in Mexico that receives tourists interested in learning the local language. Suddenly, children who today speak only Spanish began joining the classes and asking their grandparents to teach them the language, too.

For Munoz, community-based tourism can be a powerful tool for valuing cultural and regional diversity. It's about creating value over the long term — and that, he said, is where the real experience for visitors lies.
The experts agree that change is slow. But they argue it's worth the effort: If there is more respect for local people and environments, in the end, everyone goes home happier.
This article was originally written in Spanish.

articles.title: Iraqi armed group denies involvement in oil smuggling, calls probe a ‘lie’

paras.en: The Iran-aligned Kataib Hezbollah group has denied its involvement in an oil smuggling operation in Iraq’s Jurf al-Nasr area after Iraqi authorities launched an anticorruption crackdown.

Kataib Hezbollah, one of Iraq’s most heavily armed factions, said in a statement on Sunday that the Iraqi prime minister’s office was “fabricating lies” and that the group was being subjected to “the largest blackmail operation” to force its disarmament.
The statement was issued a day after Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi sacked nine senior officials following an investigation into the allegations.

The Iraqi government said an investigation committee, chaired by al-Zaidi, confirmed oil smuggling based on “intelligence documents” containing satellite images showing operations being carried out in the armed faction’s stronghold.

The committee ordered those implicated, whom it did not identify, to be referred to the judiciary and dismissed nine officials, including security and intelligence officers in Babil province, an Interior Ministry commander and the director of the Oil Pipelines Company at the Ministry of Oil.

Responding to the committee’s findings, Kataib Hezbollah said the investigation “found no violations whatsoever of the oil pipelines” and that this “definitively proves that the smuggling allegations are false”.
The group said its members accompanied the committee’s visit to the Jurf al-Nasr area on Friday.
Baghdad has been under increasing pressure from Washington to rein in Iran-aligned groups and curb Tehran’s influence in Iraq, an ally of both the US and Iran.
Al-Zaidi has previously promised to ensure that non-state armed groups would hand over their weapons to the state.
However, Kataib Hezbollah has pledged to retain its weapons arsenal and accused al-Zaidi of caving to pressure from the US, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.
Iran-aligned groups, including Kataib Hezbollah, have previously targeted US forces in Iraq and attacked Gulf states following the start of the US-Israel war on Iran in late February.
Washington accuses Tehran of using Iraq’s economy to evade sanctions and has previously sanctioned Iraqi individuals for blending Iraqi and Iranian oil.

articles.title: Widow of Haiti’s slain leader Moise to contest presidential vote

paras.en: The widow of Haiti’s slain President Jovenel Moise, whose 2021 assassination was a major turning point for the nation, has registered as a candidate for the first presidential election in a decade.
Martine Moise’s name appeared on the website of the Provisional Electoral Council (CEP) as a candidate on Sunday.
A first-round vote is set for July next year.
Haiti last held a presidential election in 2016. Successive leaders have repeatedly delayed elections, citing insecurity risks, amid the expanding influence of powerful and heavily armed gangs.
“Haiti will rise again on its own two feet, because politics needs to be done differently,” Moise, who has not publicly commented on the registration, said on X last week.
In the post, she also blamed “the opposition” for bringing the country “to its knees”. “They do not want the country to develop; they do not want the people to live well,” she said.

Martine Moise is one of three women among 33 registered presidential candidates. Among other prominent candidates are Michel Martelly and Jocelerme Privert, both former presidents, former Prime Minister Claude Joseph and former Foreign Minister Dominique Dupuy.
Several candidates, including Martelly and Privert, have been sanctioned internationally over accusations, which they both deny, of supporting armed gangs.
Martine Moise has been a key witness in the Miami court case prosecuting dozens of suspects involved in the murder of her husband, who led Haiti from 2017 until his death in July 2021.

He was shot in his bedroom by Colombian mercenaries impersonating agents of the United States Drug Enforcement Administration. Martine Moise suffered serious gunshot wounds and was flown to a hospital in Florida.
A series of transitional governments followed, as armed gangs, widely believed to be aided by corrupt politicians, seized control of much of the capital, Port-au-Prince, and surrounding regions.

About 1.5 million people have been displaced and more than 22,000 have been killed, many by security personnel. Several international forces have been deployed to Haiti to help police fight the gangs; the most recent deployment, last month, involved soldiers from El Salvador.
Last week, Haitian security forces regained control of the country’s main stadium, which had been under gang control for two years, forcing the national football team to play elsewhere.

The operation was part of a deployment of about 2,000 soldiers ordered by El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele, who announced that the troops would set up an operational base in the stadium to push further into territory still controlled by the gangs.

articles.title: US and rivals spar over next UN boss as race lurches towards deadline

paras.en: A tense race to replace outgoing United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres is heading into its final few weeks in advance of a deadline that has never been breached, as global powers spar over candidates in an opaque election process.
With eight candidates, secret polls and geopolitical rivalries at play, the choice of the UN’s next chief is still up in the air, even as Guterres must leave office on December 31.

Competing interests from the Americas to the Middle East have complicated the process, raising fears that, for the first time in history, the new year could begin without a leader at the helm of the world’s central diplomatic organisation. The late inclusion of two candidates — Emirati diplomat Lana Nusseibeh and Turkish nominee Feridun Sinirlioglu — has further split the race wide open, with no name so far succeeding in overcoming opposition from all five permanent members of the UN Security Council (UNSC), who hold vetoes.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The protracted contest is part of a “struggle over who will exercise political influence within the UN at a time when multilateralism is under considerable pressure and attack”, Georgina Holmes, senior lecturer in politics and international studies at the Open University, United Kingdom, told Al Jazeera.
“P5 member states are not as politically aligned as they have been in previous eras, arguably even during the Cold War,” said Holmes, referring to the permanent members of the UNSC.
The UN secretary-general has often been compared with a “secular pope” – a figure expected to unite countries and spearhead global diplomacy.

But the position is more than that of a figurehead. The secretary-general is also the UN’s top administrative official, responsible for tapping senior officials and supervising the UN Secretariat’s tens of thousands of staff.

“The secretary-general must be a skilled politician to navigate the geopolitics; a skilled diplomat and mediator to help settle disputes; a charismatic person in the public eye; and a solid and skilled administrator,” Jan Klabbers, professor of international law at the University of Cambridge, told Al Jazeera. “It has been called ‘the most difficult job in the world’ for a reason.”

This year’s race comes as the UN, under Guterres, is under heavy strain, having been sidelined from conflicts in Iran and Ukraine. It has faced blistering criticism from United States President Donald Trump and is suffering a financial crisis that has forced it to let go of thousands of staff.
It also comes as wider geopolitical rivalries extend to the pool of candidates to lead the organisation, who are being scrutinised over their nationalities and policy commitments.

Eight individuals who have been appointed by UN member states are currently in the running to replace Guterres. Most of them are from Latin America or the Caribbean, which is in line with representation according to informal UN protocol. Five of the eight are women, amid a push for the UN to select its first female secretary-general.
A leading contender, according to a series of anonymous straw polls the UNSC carries out to gauge support, is Costa Rican diplomat Rebeca Grynspan.

In the last poll on November 5, which does not show which UNSC members voted which way, Grynspan received 12 “encourage” votes and three “discourage” votes, according to PassBlue, a nonprofit that reports on UN affairs.

Grynspan, who heads the UN Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD), has been described as a “continuity candidate”, but there are concerns as to whether she would bring enough reform to an organisation facing huge political and financial pressures.

Richard Gowan, programme director of global issues and institutions at the International Crisis Group, told Al Jazeera that Grynspan had “solidified her position as the frontrunner”, but still appears to face opposition from the US and Russia, which could veto her bid.

While she has avoided directly confronting any veto-wielding nation, some of her reports as UNCTAD head have voiced concerns over Israel’s actions in Gaza and the occupied West Bank, positions at odds with Washington’s more full-throated support for Israel. Grynspan has previously also disagreed with Russian justifications for suspending a deal to allow the transport of grain through the Black Sea.
At the same time, she — like other candidates — is believed to be lobbying with key member states to win their support. In April, she met Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov over her candidature.
“Grynspan’s team argue that they can still nudge Washington and Moscow to accept her, and US officials do seem to be leaving open the possibility of working with her in the end,” said Gowan.

To be elected, a candidate needs at least nine votes in favour in the 15-member UNSC, while avoiding any vetoes from its five permanent members – the US, the UK, France, Russia and China. The 193-member UN General Assembly (UNGA) then ultimately has to sign off.

Ben Donaldson, adviser to the 1 for 8 Billion campaign, a civil society campaign “advocating for a fair, open, inclusive way to select the next secretary-general”, stressed that opposition from P5 members in a straw poll does not necessarily equate to an eventual veto.

“It has been used in the past as a basis to extract a concession from a candidate, very often in the form of a backroom deal to get a P5 national appointed to a key role in the future UN boss’s cabinet,” he told Al Jazeera.

The Argentinian head of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), Rafael Grossi, is also in the running. He finished second in the latest straw poll, with nine “encourage” and four “discourage” votes. However, his reputation for being closely aligned with Washington is expected to hurt him with some P5 members, especially China and Russia, though he has also had warm words for Beijing and Moscow in recent weeks.
The other candidates from Latin America or the Caribbean are Guyanese diplomat Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett, Antigua and Barbuda diplomat Maria Fernanda Espinosa and Ecuadorian diplomat Ivonne A-Baki.

Rodrigues Birkett, whose description of Israel’s actions in Gaza as “genocide” has drawn scrutiny in the US, received five “discourage” votes in the latest straw poll. Espinosa and A-Baki received 10 and 14 “discourage” votes, respectively, making their candidacies unlikely.
The UAE’s Lana Nusseibeh and Turkiye’s Feridun Sinirlioglu, nominated by their countries in recent weeks, have also shaken up the race but face significant opposition.

Nusseibeh is reportedly favoured by the US and Russia, but her candidacy has received pushback over her country’s alleged arming of paramilitary forces accused of atrocities in Sudan. The United Arab Emirates has denied the allegation. Nusseibeh received six “discourage” votes in the latest straw poll.
“Nusseibeh’s main challenge is to win over China, which has so far seemed sceptical about her candidacy,” said Gowan. “If she can get Beijing’s support, she could break through.”
Sinirlioglu’s candidature, which UNSC member Greece is expected to oppose, received eight “discourage” votes.
Ugandan politician Olara Otunnu, the only remaining African candidate, received nine “discourage” votes.
Far-right former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban, though not an official candidate, has also been floated by the US as an outside choice, The Wall Street Journal has reported.
Several analysts told Al Jazeera that Grynspan appears to be in the best position, though the influence of P5 countries could change the race.
Earlier this month, the US and Russia put their weight behind the UAE’s Nusseibeh, with France and the UK offering “little resistance”, according to diplomats cited by media platform Devex.
China, for its part, has signalled a preference for a Latin American candidate, reports The New York Times, although Beijing has not publicly endorsed anyone.

Ellen Ravndal, associate professor in political science at the University of Stavanger, Norway, told Al Jazeera the drawn-out selection process and struggle to reach consensus reflect an era of “more geopolitical tensions” and a UN that is in “near-constant crisis mode”.

Adam Day, head of the Geneva office of the United Nations University Centre for Policy Research, pointed out that while the leadership contest has been lengthier and more contested than in the previous cycles in which former Secretaries-General Guterres in 2016 and Ban Ki-moon in 2006 were elected, some earlier races stretched into December.

“In the broader scope of secretary-general races, this one is still within the range of what has been normal,” Day told Al Jazeera. “But the longer it takes, the less time the incoming secretary-general has to prepare a transition.”

If no successor to Guterres is selected by the end of the year, the UN Charter does not specify an automatic interim successor. Any gap in the post would therefore require the UNSC and other UN bodies to agree on how to manage organisational leadership and operations.

“There is widespread concern that the United States and possibly other influential states are running down the clock, potentially to increase pressure to settle for a less popular candidate or to leave the UN leaderless and weakened for a period,” said Donaldson.

articles.title: Who makes Sydney Sweeney's American Eagle jeans — and under what conditions?
articles.author: Diaa Hadid

paras.en: Who makes Sydney Sweeney's American Eagle jeans — and under what conditions?

But it's not Sweeney she recognizes — it's the jeans and jacket. This woman, a single mother, has worked on American Eagle production lines and seen those denim styles and similar models. "I know how all of them are made, because I have worked on them," she says.
The workers who make Sydney Sweeney's jeans

Workers like that single mother. She asks that we refer to her as S., the initial of her first name, because she fears her bosses at the garment factory where she works will fire her if she's identified. "If you raise your voice, they'll push you out," she says. "We are helpless."
S., a young woman, works at a factory run by a company called Artistic Garment Industries, where she says she's paid about $144 a month, a sum that supports her son and her mother.

She says the factory is "oppressively hot." It was 106 F outside when we met her, and she says the factory inside is even hotter. She says it's hard to leave her workstation to drink water because she has to meet her production targets. She says she has to check the quality of 1,000 to 1,600 pieces of clothing a day — and she's fainted three times this year. "I feel faint, and I can barely stand. I have no energy in my hands and feet," S. says. "They don't even let us sit down." But S. says she has no other options.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Artistic Garment Industries confirmed it makes clothes for American Eagle but tells NPR that it does not push out workers who complain about their working conditions. The company says it has a robust complaints system that workers can use and says it frequently checks on temperatures inside different parts of its factories.

In response to questions NPR sent to American Eagle, the company says it's "committed to working directly with our suppliers to protect the health, safety, and rights of workers. We take the concerns raised by workers — and those whom NPR interviewed — very seriously."

S. is one of around 20 workers we interviewed over the spring and summer in Bangladesh and Pakistan, two of the world's biggest global garment production hubs outside of China. Those men and women worked in five different factories. All of those workers asked NPR not to use their full names and to use only the initial of their first name, worried they'd lose their jobs or be blacklisted from future jobs if they were identified.

Although we focused on the American Eagle jeans worn by Sweeney for the 2025 campaign, the reporting led to a bigger issue: how fast fashion is made, because garment factories make clothes for multiple brands at once. Workers we met told us they made clothes for Levi's, Massimo Dutti, The Gap, H&M and American Eagle. They said it's common knowledge at the factories which brands they are making clothes for, in part because some workers are stitching on the labels.

The garment workers we spoke to offered strikingly similar accounts. And they echoed worker testimonies in multiple reports by labor and climate rights groups. The workers told us they're paid low wages, even as they're expected to reach what they say are unreasonably high production targets, often laboring in sweltering factories.

These are production targets like stitching 200 sleeves an hour or checking the quality of a thousand pieces of clothing a day. The workers we interviewed say they are unable to hydrate or cool down properly, even as extreme heat caused by climate change makes their workplaces and homes even hotter.

It can be four to six degrees hotter inside a factory, says Jason Judd, executive director of the Global Labor Institute at Cornell University, which researched heat inside garment factories and worker homes. "You've got all those bodies, all that material, all that machinery putting off heat. You've got ventilation problems."

"We're starting to see fainting, heat illness, exacerbation of chronic disease, even death," says Cara Schulte, a researcher at Climate Rights International. She authored two reports on the impacts of heat on garment workers.

Schulte says workers are put under that extreme pressure to reach production targets. A major reason is that brands demand their suppliers make enormous volumes of clothes on tight deadlines and on thin profit margins. And she says garment workers are vulnerable to the heat because they're clustered in countries like Bangladesh and Pakistan. She cites U.N. publications stating that those factories are "in areas that are warming faster than the global average, that are [already] incredibly hot and humid."
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: H&M, one of the brands that workers identified making, said it "put great effort" in ensuring fair payment to its suppliers and that labor costs are "excluded from the price negotiations of our product orders" to ensure that worker wages were not driven down.

Citing her own research, Schulte of Climate Rights International says garment workers are compelled to risk their health to survive. It's not a choice, she says. "Workers are not choosing to take these risks," she says. "They're being forced into them by poverty."

Like a woman who asks we call her R. When we met in February in the Bangladesh capital, Dhaka, R. said she was working six days a week, at least 12 hours a day, for $140 a month at a garment factory run by a company called MBM, which makes denim clothes, including for Levi's. Her job is to stitch 150 pieces of fabric per hour, which are assembled into jeans.

R. says she's considered old for a garment worker — around 40 — and says she's slowing down. She says she's berated by managers who tell her, "Why aren't you speeding up your work?" She says, "If you're short by even a single piece, you face a lot of harassment."

R. says she's managed to meet her targets so far. "Allah has kept me safe," she says. She says friends of hers who could not meet their targets were fired by the company. To reach her targets, R. says, she stays at her station throughout her shift. "Even going to the washroom has become extremely difficult."

So despite Dhaka reaching 98 F this summer, R. says she doesn't drink much water to avoid the need to take bathroom breaks. There's no AC on the factory floor, but R. says managers run ceiling fans and keep windows open.

R. says that if workers feel faint, their bosses will let them rest in a sick room for about 20 minutes. But, she says, management will terminate employment if workers say say they feel sick too often, so she pushes herself to keep going.
MBM did not respond to questions from NPR about worker allegations.

Despite the issues she raised, R. says she works in a good factory. She says the pay is higher than other garment factories. And if she's terminated, she says the company will pay the wages, including overtime, that she's owed. But she doesn't want to be let go.

These garment factories are blazing hot in part because it's expensive to retrofit them with air conditioners. A manager for MBM, who asked that NPR not use their full name because they are not authorized to speak to media, says that the company needs a brand to commit to purchasing long term in order for retrofitting the factory to pay off. The manager says no brand had committed to that kind of long-term business.

Conditions in Bangladesh are still better than in other garment hubs, because of the scrutiny after a building collapse killed more than 1,100 garment workers in 2013. Just three weeks after that disaster, a legally binding commitment called the International Accord emerged between hundreds of brands, companies and trade unions in Bangladesh to protect worker health and safety. So far, 248 global brands and retailers have signed on, covering 2.8 million workers. A version of the International Accord was established in 2023 in Pakistan but has a smaller footprint.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: There's meant to be more progress on protecting workers from extreme heat soon. Last December, the International Accord agreed to develop a protocol on heat stress. That means keeping workers cool will be an enforceable commitment for brands. For apparel companies in Bangladesh and Pakistan that have signed on to the accord, the International Accord staff will regularly inspect factories to ensure they're kept cool.

Judd, of the Global Labor Institute, says he believes there will be positive changes because the garment industry knows "they've got a problem — whether it's from a worker rights perspective, or from a business perspective, workers are slowing down, productivity is falling," he says. Either way, "you've got an interest in reducing the heat stress."

But for now, workers in Pakistan, in particular, described sweltering conditions, particularly in the port city of Karachi, one of the world's hottest garment hubs, according to the U.N.'s International Labor Organization.

In a dusty bazaar in Karachi, we met seven factory workers who mostly worked for two companies: Artistic Garment Industries — S.'s employer — and another called Artistic Milliners. Both produce clothes for big Western brands.
In their interviews with NPR, women who work, or worked, for Artistic Garment Industries described vomiting, fevers and fungal skin infections that they say were caused by the heat.

Her workday starts at 8:30 a.m. She says she is expected to work beyond her regular, nine-hour shift — often till 9 p.m. — and on Sundays as well, at some stretches. But she says she isn't paid all her overtime. I. also says supervisors on her floor berate workers if they leave their stations to drink water because it might cause them to miss their targets. So, I. says, "one person goes" to the water cooler and weathers the abuse, "fills a water bottle" and shares it with colleagues. I. says she gets about a glass full.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: I. accuses the company of "eating" her money — and her health. "They exploit us," she says.
She says she suffers from dizziness and what she describes as a sense of fatigue and weakness. She pushes herself to work: "I can't lose my job — who else will support my family?"

Artistic Garment Industries contested these claims of unhealthful and exploitative working conditions. The company told NPR that it has a robust internal complaints system that workers could, and do, use. The company says it pays all overtime and does routine checks to ensure that the heat and humidity are not excessive on the factory floor. The company says it places water stations near workers to encourage them to hydrate and says it would not tolerate supervisors who pressure workers not to drink or use the bathroom.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Workers at Artistic Milliners described hot working conditions that badly impacted women and older male workers. One woman reported constantly feeling faint but said she pushed through. The workers said their supervisors let them drink water when they needed to, but they were pressured not to use the bathroom. Some workers said they were not paid for all the overtime they worked.

A 66-year-old former worker at Artistic Milliners, Sardar, said he was let go during the pandemic but had not been given compensation owed to him by the company. When NPR met him in June, he was homeless and relied on his children for meals. When we asked if he'd ever asked for charity, he began crying: "I'd feel ashamed if people thought I was begging."

Artistic Milliners did not respond to requests for comment about statements by Sardar and other workers. Parts of the company are certified through Fair Trade USA, a nonprofit organization that certifies companies that uphold high ethical standards for treatment of workers. NPR has sought comment from Fair Trade regarding allegations made by men and women who used to work for Artistic Milliners but has not received a response.
NPR also sent detailed questions to brands that workers said they made clothes for, alongside American Eagle.
Levi Strauss & Co. says it takes "allegations of worker rights violations seriously."

Inditex, the parent company of Zara and other labels, says Artistic Milliners, which makes clothes for one of its prominent brands, Massimo Dutti, was "subject to a corrective action plan." NPR contacted Inditex for clarification on what that corrective action plan entails but did not get a response.
Gap Inc. says it is "committed to supporting the rights and safety of workers."

H&M said in an emailed response that it has "required" AGI "to develop and implement corrective action plans to address the issues identified" by NPR: "Compliance with our requirements is a condition of our business relationship." H&M also said it recognized "the increasing risks associated with extreme heat" and is part of a pilot on heat stress in Pakistan conducted by the International Accord to develop "effective and sustainable solutions."

Those big brands partly ensure working conditions in factories are up to standard through regular audits. I. and other workers tell us they regularly saw auditors visiting their garment factory floors. They also tell NPR that supervisors give them advance warning. I. says that the supervisors "tell us to say that the working conditions are better than they actually are."

Anna Bryher is part of the workers' rights group Labor Behind the Labels, which published a report in July on the "clear mismatch" in the garment industry auditing system "between what the brands are saying and believing and hearing and what the workers report." Bryher says her findings suggest that the auditing system relied on by big brands is not working.

Artistic Garment Industries says workers may have confused regular updates informing workers of their rights with being told what to say at audits. The clothing brands that NPR reached out to did not comment on allegations regarding workers being told what to say during audits.

Some workers tell NPR that their supervisors warn them that if the workers were to criticize working conditions to auditors, the companies running the factories will lose business — and that they should paint a positive picture of their workplaces. "In other words," I. says, "they ask us to lie about everything."
With additional reporting by Hanan Biswas in Dhaka, Shahzaib Wahlah in Karachi and Abdul Sattar.

articles.title: What to expect from Trump and Xi's upcoming meeting in China
articles.author: Michael Levitt

paras.en: What to expect from Trump and Xi's upcoming meeting in China
Preview of what to expect as President Trump meets with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China this week.

President Trump will meet with some of the world's most powerful leaders this week. China's Xi Jinping, Russia's Vladimir Putin and President Trump will be among the attendees to the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen China. But while the administration says nuclear proliferation is on the docket, all eyes will be on the U.S.-China relationship. That's now under serious strain after the scandalous departure of NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang, following revelations regarding a romantic relationship with a woman suspected of ties to Chinese intelligence. Evan Osnos writes for The New Yorker. He has covered China for much of his career and is closely following the APEC summit. Welcome.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: SCHMITZ: So let's start with what's been dominating headlines this week, NVIDIA. You know, this scandal is hanging over this upcoming meeting between Trump and Xi Jinping. How do you think this will set the tone?

OSNOS: Well, it is a huge development to happen right before a meeting at this altitude of two leaders. I mean, you have now a case that has brought the underlying issues right to the surface, and by that I mean the tension around technology and chips and more specifically, what the Trump administration has set out to do when it comes to allowing or restricting the export of American chips and who it's been listening to. So, you know, Jensen Huang has been one of the president's most trusted voices over the course of the last two years of this administration on technology issues. He is now gone, and so they go into this summit with a scrambled set of inputs. And it's not entirely clear how that's going to play out in the room.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: SCHMITZ: So I want to pivot to another trade issue here. This week, China extended its trade truce over rare earth exports by two more months to January 10, and for its part, the U.S. is extending tariff exclusions on 178 Chinese products until that date. What is at stake here if these two sides cannot come to an agreement?

OSNOS: Well, it's an explosive prospect. But they have managed to avoid having these full tariffs go into effect now for many months, and that's by mutual design. I mean, the - China's economy has weakness on the domestic side. They're still dealing with the outcome of a property collapse, which left 90 million houses unfilled - enough people, by the way, to house the entire population of Russia. They've had youth unemployment - at some points, up above 20%. So they were not eager to get into a trade war.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: And of course, on the United States' side, Donald Trump's party was just battered in the midterms partly because of the effects of tariffs introduced into trade relationships around the world. So in some ways, he's had reasons to try to hold this off. If, in fact, the truce collapses and they're not able to figure out a way to push this off, this could trigger another round of retaliatory tariffs and a spiral of retaliation that could drive up prices for American consumers. And that comes, obviously, at a moment when voters have signaled pretty loudly that they don't want to see that happen. So the stakes are high for the administration on that score.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: SCHMITZ: You mentioned the midterms. President Trump took, obviously, a major loss during these midterms, and come January, he's going to be facing a Democrat-controlled Congress. He's only got two years left as president. Is Xi Jinping looking beyond President Trump at this stage?

OSNOS: He doesn't have the luxury of being able to write Trump off, but he certainly does come into this meeting knowing that Trump doesn't have a tailwind. Politically, he doesn't have the kind of support in Washington that he could count on if he wanted to try to restart this tariff war. It is, in any diplomatic encounter, sort of job No. 1 - is to understand what your counterpart's vulnerabilities are. That is the thing that you're always asking your intelligence services to give you a briefing on beforehand. And in this case, Xi Jinping comes in with a knowledge of Trump's significant vulnerabilities. But he also knows, and I think this is really important to remember, that from the first term, he got a pretty clear indication that Trump can turn on a dime.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: And in the latter years of Trump's first administration, when he started to struggle after the midterms and the COVID pandemic came in and began to drag down the economy, he turned his sights on China, started blaming it for the COVID pandemic. He blamed it for his struggles in the 2020 election, and China found itself suddenly in the crosshairs. So I think the Xi Jinping cohort in the Chinese leadership has that memory, and they know that he is somebody you can't quite write off.
SCHMITZ: That is Evan Osnos. He's a staff writer for The New Yorker. Evan, thank you.
